frontmatter_description: Identify the power, status, expertise, or institutional role structure between interaction partners without choosing what they should say or do.
title: Power, Status, and Role
use_when: Use when the question asks who has authority, rank, expertise, responsibility, or role-based control in an interaction.
Use when labels such as teacher/student, manager/employee, doctor/patient, expert/novice, host/guest, parent/child, officer/citizen, or senior/junior shape how the scene is interpreted.
Use when the answer depends on whether the relation is hierarchical, peer-to-peer, advisory, supervisory, service-based, or dependency-based.
Use when a social norm follows from position or role rather than from personal liking, fairness, trust history, or group identity.
do_not_use_when: Do not use to decide the best wording, tone, apology, escalation, or persuasion strategy; route to a communication or repair unit instead.
Do not use when the main variable is whether someone is reliable over time; use Trust and Reputation.
Do not use when the main variable is whether a resource split, repayment, or burden is fair; use Fairness and Reciprocity.
Do not use when the main variable is in-group, out-group, stereotype, belonging, or identity membership; use Group Identity.
Do not use when the main variable is whether information should be kept private or disclosed; use Privacy, Secrets, and Boundaries.
trigger_checklist: Are there explicit role labels such as boss, teacher, doctor, client, officer, parent, expert, trainee, host, or guest?
Does one person have formal authority to evaluate, permit, assign, discipline, grade, hire, pay, treat, or enforce?
Does one person have recognized expertise or gatekeeping power even without formal rank?
Does the question ask how status, rank, role obligation, or institutional position changes interpretation?
Would the answer remain mostly the same if personal friendship, liking, or prior trust history were removed?
workflow: List the interaction partners and any explicit titles, roles, institutional settings, or task responsibilities.
Identify the source of asymmetry: formal authority, expertise, dependency, seniority, service role, caregiving role, or situational control.
Classify the relation as hierarchical, expert-novice, caregiver-dependent, service-provider/client, host-guest, peer, or unclear/mixed.
Separate role structure from behavior quality: a rude manager is still a manager; a kind teacher is still an evaluator.
State only the role-based relation and the norm it activates, such as deference, duty of care, evaluation power, permission control, confidentiality expectation, or obligation to follow instructions.
If the question asks what message to send or how to repair the interaction, hand off after identifying the role structure.

special_case.title: Informal familiarity does not erase formal role
special_case.rule: When people are friendly or familiar but one still holds institutional authority or expert responsibility, preserve the formal role unless the scene explicitly suspends it.

worked_example.scene: A student jokes casually with her professor after class, then asks whether she can submit the assignment late.
worked_example.question: What role structure matters here?
worked_example.answer_logic: Even though the tone is friendly, the professor still has evaluator and permission-granting authority over the student. The relevant structure is teacher/student with formal academic authority.

boundary_exit_rule: If the task asks what the lower-status or higher-status person should say, exit to a communication, persuasion, or power-distance strategy unit after naming the role.
If the task asks whether the person deserves trust because of past actions, exit to Trust and Reputation.
If the task asks whether someone took advantage, owed repayment, or split benefits unfairly, exit to Fairness and Reciprocity.
If the task asks whether an identity category, stereotype, or belonging explains interpretation, exit to Group Identity.
If the task asks whether a secret, medical fact, salary, grade, or personal detail may be shared, exit to Privacy, Secrets, and Boundaries.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when the narrow diagnostic question is: what role, rank, authority, expertise, or status relation exists between the people?
hard_boundary: This unit identifies the structure; it does not generate a tactful response.
This unit does not evaluate moral fairness except where role duties define who has authority or obligation.
This unit does not infer loyalty, reliability, or betrayal from relationship history.
This unit does not decide disclosure boundaries, though roles may help explain why a privacy expectation exists.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume the louder, older, richer, or more confident person has authority unless the scene gives a role-based reason.
Do not collapse expertise into trustworthiness; an expert role indicates knowledge authority, not necessarily honesty or goodwill.
Do not treat friendliness as equality when formal evaluation, permission, or supervision remains active.
common_failure_modes: Answering with advice about how to speak to a boss instead of identifying the boss/subordinate structure.
Confusing role power with personal preference or popularity.
Mistaking group identity, such as being from the same club or culture, for hierarchical role structure.
Ignoring temporary situational authority, such as a team captain, meeting chair, event host, or safety officer.
Over-reading status from stereotypes rather than explicit evidence in the scene.

minimal_pair.case: A nurse explains medication instructions to a patient who is unsure what to do.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The key variable is an expert/care-provider role relative to a dependent patient.

minimal_pair.case: A friend who has lied several times gives medication advice from a website.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This is a near neighbor but routes away: the key issue is reliability and source trust, not a stable role structure.

boundary_stress_test: A CEO and an intern play on the same weekend soccer team: identify whether the workplace hierarchy is active in the current scene or whether they are temporary teammates.
A junior engineer corrects a senior manager about a technical bug: separate organizational rank from domain expertise.
A teacher asks a student for help fixing a projector: the student may have technical expertise, but the teacher still holds classroom authority.
A customer yells at a cashier: customer status gives service-role expectations, not unlimited authority over the employee.
references.generalization_note: Role structure is a social-cognitive frame for interpreting obligations, authority, deference, permission, evaluation, and expertise. It should be diagnosed from explicit roles and situational powers, then handed off if the task requires communication strategy, privacy judgment, trust evaluation, or repair.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A scene names or implies roles such as manager/employee, teacher/student, expert/novice, or officer/citizen, and the question asks what relationship or authority structure matters.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: A scene includes a powerful-sounding person, but the question is about whether they are honest, fair, or liked.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A scene involves hierarchy plus a request for what to say next; this unit may identify the hierarchy but must not produce the communication plan.

notes: Keep the output focused on role diagnosis, not social strategy.
Use evidence from the scene rather than stereotypes about age, gender, class, profession, or culture.
Mixed structures are allowed: one person may have formal rank while the other has domain expertise.
core_question: Identify teacher/student, manager/subordinate, expert/novice, and related role structures
